himera.t: The first Greek city on Sicily's north coast, site of the great Greek victory over Carthage in 480 BCE and destroyed by Carthage in revenge in 409 BCE.
himera.o: Settlers from Zancle, joined by exiles from Syracuse, founded Himera in 648 BCE at the mouth of the Himera river, on Sicily's northern coast. As the westernmost Greek city on that coast, it faced the Phoenician towns of Panormus and Soloeis and the Elymians.
himera.r: Himera spoke a mixture of Chalcidian and Doric Greek and was home to the poet Stesichorus. Its tyrant Terillus was expelled by Theron of Acragas around 483 BCE and appealed to Carthage. In 480 BCE Gelon of Syracuse and Theron crushed the Carthaginian army of Hamilcar outside the city, and the Victory Temple was built in thanks. Theron's son then governed Himera, and later it was a democracy.
himera.e: In 409 BCE Hannibal Mago, grandson of Hamilcar, took Himera, razed it and is said to have executed 3,000 prisoners on the spot where his grandfather had died. Survivors and Carthaginian settlers founded Thermae Himeraeae nearby in 407 BCE. The ruins and battlefield cemeteries have been excavated.

hermione.t: Coastal city of the southern Argolid, known for its sanctuary of Demeter Chthonia and its purple dye.
hermione.o: Hermione lay on a peninsula at the southern tip of the Argolid, facing the islands of Hydra and Spetses. Greek tradition held that its first people were Dryopes, later joined by Dorians from Argos in the early Iron Age.
hermione.r: Hermione was a small independent city living from fishing, farming and the production of purple dye from murex shells. Its sanctuary of Demeter Chthonia had a festival with a famous cattle sacrifice, and a nearby chasm was believed to be a short route to the underworld. The city sent ships to Salamis in 480 BCE and was usually a member of the Peloponnesian League.
hermione.e: Hermione joined the Achaean League c. 229 BCE when its tyrant Xenon stepped down, and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE. The modern town of Ermioni occupies the site.
hermione.re: Greek religion; cult of Demeter Chthonia

hitu.t: A Muslim clove-trading state on the north coast of Ambon, whose long war with the Dutch East India Company ended in 1646.
hitu.o: Hitu was a federation of villages on the northern peninsula of Ambon Island, led by four chiefs called perdana. Its chronicle, the Hikayat Tanah Hitu written by Imam Rijali in the mid-17th century, traces its rulers to settlers from Java and the Moluccas. Hitu's leaders accepted Islam in the late 15th century through ties with Javanese ports and Giri Kedaton.
hitu.r: Hitu grew rich selling cloves to Javanese and Malay merchants and kept close links with Ternate and Makassar. Its council of chiefs governed through village heads. In 1600 Hitu allied with the Dutch against the Portuguese, but soon resisted the Company's attempts to monopolise the clove trade.
hitu.e: The Hitu war, led by Kakiali until his murder in 1643, ended in 1646 when the Dutch took the mountain fortress of Kapahaha. Hitu's leaders were absorbed into the colonial village system, and the Hikayat Tanah Hitu remains a key Malay source for Moluccan history.

hasmonean-kingdom.t: The Hasmonean Kingdom, the independent Jewish state founded by the Maccabees, whose victory is still celebrated at Hanukkah.
hasmonean-kingdom.o: In 167 BCE Antiochus IV of the Seleucid Empire banned Jewish practices, provoking a revolt led by the priest Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees. Judas recaptured the Temple in 164 BCE. By 140 BCE his brother Simon had won full independence and was confirmed as high priest and ruler.
hasmonean-kingdom.r: Hasmonean rulers combined the high priesthood with political power, and from Aristobulus I took the title king. John Hyrcanus conquered Idumaea and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim; Alexander Jannaeus extended the realm across the Jordan. Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes emerged in this era.
hasmonean-kingdom.e: Civil war between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II invited Pompey of the Roman Republic, who took Jerusalem in 63 BCE. Antigonus regained the throne with Parthian help in 40 BCE, but Herod captured Jerusalem in 37 BCE, founding the Herodian Kingdom of Judea.

hsenwi-state.t: A powerful northern Shan state on the Burma-China frontier, at times a major Tai power, later split by the British into North and South Hsenwi.
hsenwi-state.o: Hsenwi, Shan Theinni, emerged as one of the principal Shan states of the northern plateau, with a ruling house that Shan tradition dates to the 13th or 14th century and links to Mong Mao. It controlled routes between the Irrawaddy valley and Yunnan.
hsenwi-state.r: Hsenwi's saophas ruled a large territory of Shan, Kachin, Palaung and Wa peoples, trading tea, cotton and silver along the caravan routes to China. Ming China called it Muban and recognised its ruler as a pacification commissioner, while Burmese kings from Bayinnaung onward claimed overlordship. Succession disputes were common.
hsenwi-state.e: In the 1880s Hsenwi was torn by civil war among rival claimants to the saopha title. After the British annexation of Upper Burma, the state was divided in 1888 into North Hsenwi and South Hsenwi, which survived as separate Shan states until 1959.

helvetic-republic.t: France's centralised sister republic in Switzerland, which abolished the old cantons and subject lands and introduced equal citizenship.
helvetic-republic.o: French troops invaded the Old Swiss Confederacy in early 1798, and Bern fell in March. On 12 April 1798 a constitution drafted by Peter Ochs of Basel proclaimed the Helvetic Republic, one and indivisible, with its first capital at Aarau.
helvetic-republic.r: The republic abolished the subject territories and created equal citizenship, freedom of religion and the press, and a single currency, the franc. Its directory and legislature replaced the old cantons with administrative units. Minister Philipp Albert Stapfer planned public schooling. But French requisitions, conscription and the suppression of resistance in Nidwalden made it unpopular, and the capital moved to Lucerne and then Bern.
helvetic-republic.e: Repeated coups and a federalist uprising in 1802 led Napoleon to impose the Act of Mediation in 1803, restoring cantons in a new Swiss Confederation. Its legacy includes the equality of cantons and the abolition of subject lands.

hong-kong-british.t: The British colony on the south China coast that grew from a small island trading post into one of the world's great financial centres before its return to China in 1997.
hong-kong-british.o: British forces occupied Hong Kong Island in January 1841 during the First Opium War, and the Treaty of Nanking ceded it to Britain in 1842. Kowloon was added in 1860, and in 1898 the New Territories were leased for ninety-nine years, giving the colony its final shape within the British Empire.
hong-kong-british.r: A governor ruled with appointed councils, and the colony thrived as a free port and entrepôt for the China trade. Japan occupied it from 1941 to 1945. After 1949 refugees from mainland China fuelled a manufacturing boom, and from the 1970s Hong Kong became a major financial centre. Governor Murray MacLehose expanded housing and created the anti-corruption commission in 1974.
hong-kong-british.e: Because the New Territories lease expired in 1997, Britain and China signed the Joint Declaration in 1984. Governor Chris Patten introduced late electoral reforms, and on 1 July 1997 Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China.

hikone-domain.t: The domain of the Ii family on Lake Biwa, pillars of the Tokugawa order whose head Ii Naosuke opened Japan to Western trade.
hikone-domain.o: Ii Naomasa, one of Tokugawa Ieyasu's most trusted generals and leader of the red-armoured troops, was given the former lands of Ishida Mitsunari at Sawayama after Sekigahara in 1600. After his death in 1602 his sons built Hikone castle nearby, completed in 1622.
hikone-domain.r: The Ii, hereditary vassals of the Tokugawa with up to 350,000 koku, guarded the approach to Kyoto and supplied several great elders (tairo) to the shogunate. Ii Naosuke, tairo from 1858, signed the treaty with the United States without imperial approval and purged opponents in the Ansei purge.
hikone-domain.e: Naosuke was assassinated at the Sakurada Gate in 1860 and the domain was reduced. In 1868 Hikone switched to the imperial side. After abolition in 1871 it became part of Shiga Prefecture; Hikone castle is a national treasure.

habsburg-spain.t: The Spanish monarchy under the Habsburgs, the greatest power in 16th-century Europe and the age of the Spanish Golden Age.
habsburg-spain.o: In 1516 Charles I, grandson of Ferdinand II and Isabella I and of Emperor Maximilian I, inherited the Crown of Castile and the Crown of Aragon. Elected Holy Roman Emperor in 1519, he united Spain with the Low Countries, Italian lands and the conquests of the Spanish Empire in the Americas.
habsburg-spain.r: The monarchy was a composite of kingdoms, each with its own laws, governed through councils from Madrid, the capital from 1561. American silver financed wars against France, the Ottomans and Protestant powers. Philip II built the Escorial, but faced the Dutch revolt and lost the Armada of 1588. Cervantes, Velázquez and Lope de Vega defined the Golden Age.
habsburg-spain.e: Repeated bankruptcies, the revolts of 1640 and defeats such as Rocroi in 1643 marked decline. The childless Charles II died in 1700, leaving the throne to Philip of Anjou, which led to the War of the Spanish Succession and Bourbon Spain.

huexotzinco.t: A Nahua altepetl on the eastern slopes of Iztaccíhuatl that remained independent of the Aztecs and fought them in ritual 'flower wars'.
huexotzinco.o: Huexotzinco (modern Huejotzingo) was settled by Chichimec and Nahua groups in the Puebla valley in the 12th or 13th century, and grew into a powerful city-state that at times dominated neighbours such as Tlaxcala and Cholula.
huexotzinco.r: It was governed by a ruler (tlatoani) and nobles over a farming population in a well-watered valley. With Tlaxcala and Cholula it formed an independent bloc east of the volcanoes, waging the ritualised xochiyaoyotl (flower wars) with the Aztec Empire, in which warriors sought captives for sacrifice. In the early 16th century it suffered defeats by Tlaxcala and sought Aztec help.
huexotzinco.e: Huexotzinco joined the Spanish against Tenochtitlan in 1519-21. Its nobles later sent a famous 1560 letter to Philip II protesting excessive tribute. Its Franciscan monastery is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

heshun-confederation.t: Federation of Hakka Chinese gold-mining companies in West Borneo that governed its own territory for nearly 80 years.
heshun-confederation.o: From the mid 18th century Malay rulers such as the Sambas Sultanate invited Chinese miners to work the gold fields of western Borneo. The miners organised themselves into kongsis, partnerships that held land and shares, and in 1776 fourteen kongsis around Monterado formed the Heshun federation, dominated by the Dagang kongsi.
heshun-confederation.r: The kongsis governed themselves through elected leaders and assemblies of shareholders, collected taxes, ran courts and schools, and kept armed forces. Their towns had temples, farms and markets, and they paid little more than nominal tribute to the Malay sultans. Rivalry with the Lanfang Republic and among member kongsis was frequent.
heshun-confederation.e: Expanding Dutch rule in the 19th century clashed with the kongsis over taxes and trade. In the Kongsi Wars of 1850 to 1854 Dutch forces defeated Heshun and dissolved the federation. Many Hakka communities in West Kalimantan descend from its miners.

hordaland.t: Petty kingdom around the fjords of modern Bergen, remembered in saga tradition for resisting Harald Fairhair's unification of Norway.
hordaland.o: Hordaland, the coast and fjords around what is now Bergen, was a populous district of western Norway in the Iron Age. The sagas describe it as a kingdom in the 9th century, ruled by local kings with fleets and many retainers.
hordaland.r: Its people farmed, fished and sailed; many western Norwegian raiders and settlers of the Viking Age came from here. Hordaland belonged to the Gulating law province. According to Snorri, Harald Fairhair vowed not to cut his hair until he ruled all Norway after Gyda, daughter of a Hordaland king, refused to marry a petty king.
hordaland.e: Its kings joined the coalition defeated by Harald at Hafrsfjord, traditionally around 872, and Hordaland became part of the Kingdom of Norway. Bergen, founded in the 11th century, grew into medieval Norway's chief town.

harhar.t: A Zagros town on the main road into Iran, captured by Sargon II in 716 BCE and refounded as the Assyrian provincial capital Kar-Sharrukin.
harhar.o: Harhar lay in the central Zagros, probably in the Kermanshah region, at a key point on the route from Mesopotamia to the Iranian plateau. It appears in Assyrian sources in the 8th century BCE as a fortified town ruled by local lords in the borderland where Median groups were settling.
harhar.r: Almost nothing is known of its own government. Assyrian texts say that the people of Harhar drove out a ruler installed by Assyria and turned to Dalta of Ellipi, prompting Sargon II to intervene. Its value lay in the trade in horses and goods moving along the road between the plateau and the lowlands.
harhar.e: In 716 BCE Sargon II took Harhar, settled deportees there and renamed it Kar-Sharrukin, 'Fort Sargon', as the capital of a new Assyrian province facing the Medes. It remained an Assyrian outpost until Median expansion in the 7th century BCE.

hadejia-emirate.t: A north-eastern emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate, remembered for the rebel emir Buhari and for being one of the last emirates to fight the British.
hadejia-emirate.o: Hadejia arose from the jihad in the borderlands between Hausaland and the Kanem-Bornu Empire, where Fulani clans took control of the old Hausa town of Hadejia around 1808. Its first emirs received their authority from Sokoto and fought Bornu, the Kanuri-speaking local populations and their neighbours in Katagum.
hadejia-emirate.r: Hadejia lay on the fertile floodplains of the Hadejia river, farming grain and raising cattle. The emir ruled through titled officials. Under Emir Buhari, who reigned in 1848-1850 and again from 1851 to 1863, Hadejia rebelled against Sokoto, defeated punitive expeditions and raided its neighbours, before returning to allegiance after his death.
hadejia-emirate.e: Hadejia submitted to the British in 1903 but resisted their authority, and in 1906 British troops stormed the town; Emir Muhammadu was killed. It then became part of Northern Nigeria, and the Emir of Hadejia still reigns in Jigawa State.

hamidids.t: A Turkish beylik of the Lakes Region of south-western Anatolia, ruled from Egirdir, whose sale of lands helped the Ottomans expand.
hamidids.o: Felek al-Din Dundar Bey, grandson of Hamid Bey, a Turkmen commander of the Seljuks, established himself around Egirdir and Isparta at the beginning of the 14th century. A branch of the family took Antalya and became the Teke beylik.
hamidids.r: The Hamidids ruled the lake district around Egirdir, Isparta, Burdur and Uluborlu, a land of orchards and pastures on the routes between Konya and the coast. Dundar Bey was executed in 1324 by the Ilkhanid governor Timurtash, but the family returned after he fell. The beylik built mosques and turned a Seljuk caravanserai in Egirdir into a madrasa.
hamidids.e: In 1374 Kemal al-Din Husayn Bey sold several towns, including Beysehir and Aksehir, to the Ottoman sultan Murad I. Bayezid I annexed the rest in 1391.

hephthalite-empire.t: The 'White Huns' who ruled Bactria and Sogdiana for a century, killed a Persian king in battle and forced Sasanian Persia to pay them tribute.
hephthalite-empire.o: The Hephthalites rose in the region of the upper Amu Darya and Bactria in the mid-5th century, perhaps as a vassal people of the Rouran. They drove out the Kidarite Kingdom and fought the Sasanians, defeating and capturing Peroz I and then killing him in battle in 484.
hephthalite-empire.r: From their capital at Kunduz they ruled a loose empire from Sogdiana to the Tarim oases and the Hindu Kush, with Bactrian as the administrative language. Byzantine writer Procopius called them 'White Huns' and described them as more settled than other Huns, with a single king and laws. They held Kavad I's Sasanian throne in their gift and collected tribute from Persia, and Sogdian cities prospered on trade.
hephthalite-empire.e: Between about 557 and 560 the Turkic Khaganate under Istämi, allied with the Sasanian Khosrow I, crushed the Hephthalites near Bukhara. Their lands were divided along the Amu Darya, and Hephthalite principalities survived in Tokharistan under Turkic rule, later the Yabghus of Tokharistan.

hatay-state.t: A transitional state created from the Sanjak of Alexandretta in 1938, which joined Turkey within a year.
hatay-state.o: After elections held under Turkish military supervision gave Turks a majority, the assembly of the Sanjak of Alexandretta proclaimed the State of Hatay in September 1938, with Antakya (Antioch) as capital. France, seeking Turkish support against Germany, accepted the change.
hatay-state.r: Tayfur Sokmen was elected head of state and Abdurrahman Melek prime minister. The state used a flag modelled on Turkey's, adopted Turkish laws and currency and was closely tied to Ankara, functioning as a stage towards annexation rather than as an independent country.
hatay-state.e: On 29 June 1939 the assembly voted to join Turkey, which formally annexed Hatay in July. Many Armenians and Arabs left for Syria and Lebanon, including the Armenians of Musa Dagh, who resettled at Anjar.

habsburg-monarchy.t: The composite realm of the Austrian Habsburgs, formed in 1526 when Austria was joined with Bohemia and Hungary, which grew into a great power on the Danube.
habsburg-monarchy.o: After King Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia died at Mohács in 1526, his brother-in-law Archduke Ferdinand of Austria was elected king of both realms. This union of the Archduchy of Austria and the other hereditary lands with the Kingdom of Bohemia and Hungary created the Habsburg Monarchy, though most of Hungary lay under Ottoman rule for some 150 years.
habsburg-monarchy.r: There was no single state: each kingdom and duchy kept its own estates, laws and diets, bound together by the dynasty, the army and Catholicism, which was imposed after the Bohemian revolt was crushed at the White Mountain in 1620. The Ottomans were driven from Vienna in 1683 and Hungary was reconquered by 1699. Maria Theresa and Joseph II centralised administration, taxation and schooling in the 18th century.
habsburg-monarchy.e: In answer to Napoleon's imperial title, Francis II proclaimed the Austrian Empire in 1804, giving the monarchy a single name and crown; two years later he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire. The monarchy continued as Austria-Hungary until 1918.

han-song.t: The Red Turban 'Song' dynasty of Han Lin'er, the millenarian rebel state under whose banner Zhu Yuanzhang rose to found the Ming.
han-song.o: Han Shantong, a White Lotus leader who preached the coming of the Buddha Maitreya and claimed descent from the Song emperors, launched the Red Turban revolt against the Yuan Dynasty in 1351 but was killed. In 1355 his general Liu Futong enthroned Han Shantong's son Han Lin'er as emperor of a restored Song at Bozhou in Anhui.
han-song.r: The state was a loose coalition of Red Turban armies rather than a settled government, inspired by Maitreya and Manichaean-influenced beliefs in a coming 'King of Light'. Liu Futong held real power and in 1358 took Kaifeng, the old Song capital, while other columns burned the Yuan summer capital Shangdu and raided into Goryeo. Zhu Yuanzhang at Nanjing was nominally one of its commanders.
han-song.e: Yuan forces retook Kaifeng in 1359, and in 1363 troops of Zhang Shicheng killed Liu Futong at Anfeng. Zhu Yuanzhang rescued Han Lin'er, who drowned in the Yangtze in 1366 while being brought to Nanjing, probably on Zhu's orders. Zhu soon founded the Ming Empire.

haushabi-sultanate.t: A small tribal sultanate on the road between Aden and Ta'izz, one of the British-protected states of the Aden hinterland.
haushabi-sultanate.o: The Haushabi tribe held the valleys north of the Sultanate of Lahej, on the main route from Aden into the Yemeni highlands. Its sultans, based at Musaymir, emerged as independent rulers in the 18th century as the Qasimid State lost control of the south.
haushabi-sultanate.r: The sultanate was a small tribal territory with little central administration, living from farming and dues on caravans. Its position near the frontier with Ottoman, later imamic, Yemen made it a concern for the British, who brought it into the Aden Protectorate through treaties in the late 19th century. It joined the Federation of South Arabia.
haushabi-sultanate.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over the area, and the sultanate was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

hungarian-state-1849.t: Independent Hungary proclaimed in Debrecen during the revolution of 1848 to 1849, which dethroned the Habsburgs and was crushed by Austrian and Russian armies.
hungarian-state-1849.o: Hungary's revolution of 1848 began with the April Laws, but by winter the court in Vienna was at war with the Hungarian government. After the spring campaign drove back Austrian forces, the Hungarian parliament, meeting in Debrecen, adopted the Declaration of Independence on 14 April 1849, deposing the Habsburg dynasty and electing Lajos Kossuth governor-president.
hungarian-state-1849.r: The new state left the question of monarchy or republic undecided. Kossuth headed the state, Bertalan Szemere's government ran affairs, and the honvéd army under commanders such as Artúr Görgei recaptured Buda in May 1849. Paper money, the Kossuth notes, financed the war. Relations with Romanian, Serb and Croat minorities stayed hostile until a late nationalities law in July.
hungarian-state-1849.e: Russian intervention in June 1849 tipped the balance, and Görgei surrendered at Világos on 13 August. Thirteen generals were executed at Arad in October, and Kossuth went into exile. Neo-absolutist rule followed until the Compromise of 1867.

hunza-state.t: A Karakoram principality on the old route to Kashgar, once feared for its caravan raids, whose Mirs ruled from Baltit Fort until 1974.
hunza-state.o: The Mirs of Hunza, of the Ayash dynasty, trace their line to a ruler who, by local tradition, divided the valley with his brother, the ancestor of the Mirs of Nagar. The register's start date is approximate. Baltit Fort, the royal seat, is several centuries old.
hunza-state.r: Hunza's Burushaski-speaking people farmed irrigated terraces and, until the late 19th century, raided caravans on the routes between Ladakh and Yarkand. The Mirs sent tribute to the Qing emperors of China while dealing with Kashmir. Most people became Ismaili Muslims. In 1891 a British force defeated Hunza and Nagar; Mir Safdar Ali Khan fled to China, and his half-brother Muhammad Nazim Khan was installed.
hunza-state.e: Mir Muhammad Jamal Khan acceded to Pakistan in 1947. The principality was abolished in 1974. The Karakoram Highway now runs through the valley, and Baltit Fort is a museum.

habesh-eyalet.t: The Ottoman province on the Red Sea coasts of Eritrea, Sudan and Arabia, created to fight the Portuguese and control the trade of the Horn.
habesh-eyalet.o: After Portuguese fleets entered the Red Sea, the Ottomans sent Ozdemir Pasha, who in 1555 created the province of Habesh (Abyssinia) and in 1557 seized Massawa and the Dahlak islands from the Sultanate of Dahlak. He hoped to conquer the Ethiopian highlands, and the province's seat moved between Massawa, Suakin and later Jeddah.
habesh-eyalet.r: The Ottomans held the coast, collecting customs from the Red Sea trade, and allied at times with Medri Bahri against the Ethiopian emperors. Inland campaigns failed after Sarsa Dengel's victories in the 1570s and 1580s. Day-to-day authority on the African coast passed to the Naibs of Arkiko, local Beja governors who ruled in the sultan's name.
habesh-eyalet.e: The province was much reduced over time, and in 1865 the Ottomans transferred Massawa and Suakin to Khedive Ismail's Egypt. The Italians later took Massawa in 1885, a step towards Italian Eritrea.

hyderabad-state.t: The Nizam's dominions in the Deccan, the largest and richest princely state of India, ruled by the Asaf Jahi dynasty until Operation Polo in 1948.
hyderabad-state.o: Qamar-ud-din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, defeated a rival at Shakar Kheda in 1724 and made himself effectively independent, while still nominally serving Delhi. Taking the title Asaf Jah, he founded a dynasty first based at Aurangabad; Nizam Ali Khan moved the capital to Hyderabad in 1763.
hyderabad-state.r: The Nizams allied with the East India Company, accepting a subsidiary alliance in 1798 and later assigning Berar to the British. A Muslim, Urdu-speaking court governed a largely Hindu population speaking Telugu, Marathi and Kannada. The state had its own currency, railways and postal service. Mir Osman Ali Khan, reputed the richest man in the world, founded Osmania University in 1918 with Urdu as its medium.
hyderabad-state.e: Osman Ali Khan sought to stay independent in 1947. Amid Razakar violence and the Telangana peasant uprising, India invaded in September 1948 (Operation Polo) and annexed the state. Hyderabad State continued within India until it was divided on linguistic lines in 1956.

herodian-ethnarchy-of-judea.t: The short reign of Herod Archelaus over Judea, Samaria and Idumaea, whose failure led Rome to rule Judea directly through prefects.
herodian-ethnarchy-of-judea.o: Herod the Great's will named Archelaus as heir to the kingship, but Augustus in 4 BCE gave him only the title ethnarch and the heartland of the kingdom: Judea with Jerusalem, Samaria and Idumaea, about half of his father's territory, with the promise of a crown if he governed well.
herodian-ethnarchy-of-judea.r: His reign began with the killing of some three thousand people when he suppressed a Passover protest in the Temple courts, and further revolts had to be crushed by the Syrian governor Varus. Archelaus founded the village of Archelais, planted palms near Jericho and rebuilt the palace there. His marriage to Glaphyra, widow of his half-brother, offended religious opinion.
herodian-ethnarchy-of-judea.e: In 6 CE a joint delegation of Judeans and Samaritans complained to Augustus, who deposed Archelaus and exiled him to Vienne in Gaul. Judea became a Roman province under equestrian prefects, and the census of Quirinius that followed provoked the revolt of Judas of Galilee.

hirpini.t: Samnite people of the southern Apennines, named after the wolf that legend says led them, who resisted Rome until the Social War.
hirpini.o: The Hirpini lived in the mountains of modern Irpinia, east of Campania. Their name was explained from the Oscan word hirpus, 'wolf', after the animal that guided their ancestors in a 'sacred spring' migration from the Sabine lands. They were one of the peoples of the Samnite League.
hirpini.r: Their centres included Maleventum (later Beneventum), Aeclanum, Compsa and Abellinum. They lived from herding and farming in upland valleys, and the sanctuary of the goddess Mefitis in the Ansanto valley, by sulphurous springs, was a major cult site. As part of Samnium they fought Rome in the Samnite Wars.
hirpini.e: After the Samnite defeat Rome founded Beneventum on Hirpine land in 268 BCE. The Hirpini went over to Hannibal after Cannae and were punished. They joined the Italian revolt in 91 BCE; Sulla took Aeclanum in 89 BCE, after which they submitted and received citizenship.

habsburg-netherlands.t: The Low Countries under Maximilian, Philip the Handsome and Charles V, gathered into the Seventeen Provinces and bound to the Habsburg world empire.
habsburg-netherlands.o: Mary of Burgundy's death in 1482 left the Burgundian State's northern lands to her infant son Philip the Handsome, with her widower Maximilian of Austria as regent. Maximilian fought rebellious Flemish towns and France for a decade before Philip came of age in 1494.
habsburg-netherlands.r: Charles V, born at Ghent in 1500, rounded off the territories by taking Frisia, Utrecht, Overijssel, Groningen and Guelders, forming the Seventeen Provinces. Regents Margaret of Austria and Mary of Hungary governed from Mechelen and Brussels with the States General and collateral councils. Antwerp became Europe's main market, and Erasmus worked in Leuven. The Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 made the provinces one indivisible inheritance.
habsburg-netherlands.e: Charles V abdicated in Brussels in 1555, handing the Netherlands to his son Philip II. Philip's rule from Spain began the Spanish Netherlands, and his religious and fiscal policies provoked the Dutch Revolt.

high-kingship-of-ireland.t: The prestigious title of king of Tara and over-king of Ireland, contested for centuries by the Ui Neill and later by provincial dynasties such as Brian Boru's.
high-kingship-of-ireland.o: The kingship of Tara, an ancient royal site in Meath, was claimed from the 6th century by the Ui Neill dynasties, who presented it as an ancient kingship of all Ireland. Their northern and southern branches alternated the title for several centuries, though actual authority rarely reached beyond the northern half of the island.
high-kingship-of-ireland.r: The high king was an overlord rather than a ruler of a centralised state: he took hostages and tribute from provincial kings and held the Feis Temro and fairs. Monastic chroniclers and law tracts built up the ideology of a sacred kingship. Real power depended on military success.
high-kingship-of-ireland.e: Brian Boru of Munster broke the Ui Neill monopoly around 1002, and later kings ruled 'with opposition'. Ruaidri Ua Conchobair, the last high king, submitted to Henry II after the Norman invasion of 1171 and the Lordship of Ireland; he died in 1198.

hiraab-imamate.t: A Somali clan state that rose on the ruins of the Ajuran Sultanate and dominated Mogadishu and the central Somali coast for nearly two centuries.
hiraab-imamate.o: In the late 17th century the Hiraab clans of the Hawiye, among them the Abgaal and Habar Gidir, revolted against the Ajuran Sultanate. The Hiraab established an imamate, with the imam drawn from the Abgaal and military leadership from allied lineages, taking control of Mogadishu and the coast north of it.
hiraab-imamate.r: The imamate was a clan confederation rather than a bureaucratic state. The imam held religious and political authority, mediated disputes under Somali customary law and Islamic law, and drew revenues from the coastal trade in livestock, grain and ivory. Mogadishu itself was split between rival quarters, Shingani and Hamar Weyne.
hiraab-imamate.e: The imamate weakened in the 19th century as the Sultanate of the Geledi rose inland and the Sultanate of Zanzibar asserted authority over Mogadishu in the 1870s. The area later became part of Italian Somaliland.

hungarian-democratic-republic.t: Hungary's first republic, born of the Aster Revolution of 1918, which collapsed under the pressure of defeat and territorial losses.
hungarian-democratic-republic.o: As Austria-Hungary collapsed at the end of the First World War, the Aster Revolution in Budapest on 31 October 1918 brought Count Mihály Károlyi to power as prime minister; on the same day former premier István Tisza was murdered. On 16 November 1918 the National Council proclaimed Hungary a republic, ending the Kingdom of Hungary (1867-1918).
hungarian-democratic-republic.r: Károlyi's coalition of liberals, radicals and Social Democrats introduced universal suffrage and began land reform, distributing his own estate. But it faced economic chaos, returning soldiers and the advance of Czechoslovak, Romanian and Serbian troops beyond the Belgrade armistice lines. Károlyi became provisional president in January 1919, with Dénes Berinkey as prime minister.
hungarian-democratic-republic.e: In March 1919 the Allies' Vix Note demanded a further Hungarian withdrawal in the east. Károlyi's government resigned, and the Social Democrats united with the Communists, who proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic on 21 March 1919.

hamath.t: Hamath, a Syrian kingdom on the Orontes whose kings led resistance to Assyria at Qarqar and left both Luwian and Aramaic inscriptions.
hamath.o: Hamath, modern Hama, rose after the Late Bronze Age collapse as a kingdom on the middle Orontes. Its early rulers wrote in Luwian hieroglyphs; carved stones from the city, noticed by Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in 1812, were the first Hittite hieroglyphs known to modern scholars.
hamath.r: Under King Urhilina, Hamath joined Aram-Damascus and the Kingdom of Israel to fight Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BCE. Around 800 BCE the usurper Zakkur ruled Hamath and Lu'ash, and his Aramaic stele tells how the god Baalshamin saved him from a siege by a coalition led by Aram-Damascus.
hamath.e: Hamath became a tributary of the Assyrian Empire. In 720 BCE Yau-bidi led a revolt; Sargon II defeated him at Qarqar, flayed him, and annexed Hamath as a province, deporting many of its people.

hungarian-peoples-republic.t: Communist Hungary, from Rákosi's Stalinism and the crushed revolution of 1956 to János Kádár's relatively relaxed 'goulash communism'.
hungarian-peoples-republic.o: After the communists eliminated their rivals in the Second Hungarian Republic, a Soviet-style constitution proclaimed the Hungarian People's Republic on 20 August 1949. Mátyás Rákosi, leader of the Hungarian Working People's Party, ruled as a Stalinist dictator, with show trials such as that of László Rajk and a feared secret police, the ÁVH.
hungarian-peoples-republic.r: After Stalin's death Imre Nagy eased repression, and on 23 October 1956 a popular revolution brought him back to power and declared neutrality. Soviet forces crushed it in November, and János Kádár ruled for over thirty years. After harsh reprisals, Kádár allowed a mixed economy under the New Economic Mechanism of 1968, making Hungary the most liberal state in the Soviet bloc.
hungarian-peoples-republic.e: Economic problems and reformers in the party removed Kádár in 1988. In 1989 Round Table talks agreed free elections, Imre Nagy was solemnly reburied, and the border with Austria was opened. On 23 October 1989 the Republic of Hungary was proclaimed.

hanthawaddy-kingdom.t: The Mon kingdom of Lower Myanmar, centred on Martaban and later Pegu, that grew rich on Indian Ocean trade and held off Ava for over a century.
hanthawaddy-kingdom.o: After the fall of the Pagan Kingdom, Wareru, a Mon adventurer said to have been a merchant, seized Martaban in 1287 and gained recognition from Sukhothai. His dynasty united the Mon-speaking coast of Ramannadesa, and in 1369 King Binnya U moved the capital to Pegu, also called Hanthawaddy.
hanthawaddy-kingdom.r: The kingdom's ports, Martaban, Pegu, Bassein and Syriam, exported rice, lac, rubies and the famous Martaban jars across the Bay of Bengal. Razadarit fought the Forty Years' War with the Ava Kingdom from 1385 to 1424 and kept Hanthawaddy independent. Queen Shin Sawbu and her successor Dhammazedi, a former monk, presided over a golden age; Dhammazedi reformed the Buddhist order through the Kalyani inscriptions.
hanthawaddy-kingdom.e: Internal decline left Hanthawaddy open to the rising First Toungoo Empire, whose king Tabinshwehti took Pegu in 1539 and Martaban in 1541, making Pegu his own capital. Mon resistance revived in the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom of the 18th century.

heraclea-pontica.t: Powerful Greek city on the southern Black Sea coast, known for its serf-like Mariandynian subjects, its philosopher-tyrants and its own daughter colonies.
heraclea-pontica.o: Heraclea was founded c. 560 BCE by settlers from Megara joined by Boeotians, on the coast of north-west Anatolia where Heracles was said to have descended to the underworld. The colonists subdued the local Mariandynians, who became a dependent rural population compared by ancient writers to the helots of Sparta.
heraclea-pontica.r: Heraclea controlled a wide territory, a strong fleet and trade in grain, timber and nuts, and founded Chersonesus Taurica in Crimea. Its oligarchy gave way in 364 BCE to the tyranny of Clearchus, a former pupil of Plato and Isocrates, and his family. His widowed daughter-in-law Amastris ruled and later married Lysimachus. The local historian Memnon preserved its story.
heraclea-pontica.e: After the tyranny ended, Heraclea regained independence, allied with Rome and later with Mithridates VI of Pontus. In the Third Mithridatic War the Roman commander Marcus Aurelius Cotta took and sacked it in 70 BCE. It recovered under Roman rule and survives as the Turkish town of Karadeniz Eregli.

hintata-emirate.t: The Masmuda Berber emirs of Marrakesh who ruled southern Morocco after the Marinid collapse, until the rising Saadis took their city.
hintata-emirate.o: The Hintata were a leading Masmuda Berber tribe of the High Atlas, prominent since Almohad times. Under the Marinid Sultanate their chiefs served as governors of Marrakesh. When Marinid authority collapsed in 1465 the Hintata emirs became de facto independent rulers of the city and the Haouz plain.
hintata-emirate.r: The emirs governed a region of Atlas tribes and plains agriculture from the old imperial capital. They dealt with the Portuguese posts at Safi and Azemmour and are described by Leo Africanus, who visited in the early 16th century. Power rested on tribal alliances rather than a strong administration.
hintata-emirate.e: The Saadi Sultanate, rising in the Sous, pressed northward. The last important emir, Muhammad ibn Nasir Bu Shentuf, was assassinated in 1524, and the Saadis entered Marrakesh around 1525, making it their capital.

hokuzan.t: The northern kingdom of 14th-century Okinawa, centred on the great stone castle of Nakijin, conquered by Chuzan in 1416.
hokuzan.o: Hokuzan arose in the early 14th century in the mountainous north of Okinawa and the Motobu peninsula, one of three rival kingdoms that formed as local lords consolidated power. Its seat was Nakijin, whose long, winding stone walls survive as a World Heritage Site.
hokuzan.r: Hokuzan was the largest of the three kingdoms in area but the poorest in farmland. Its kings Haniji, Min and Hananchi sent tribute missions to Ming China from 1383, and the castle has yielded Chinese ceramics that show active trade. Power rested on alliances with local aji lords.
hokuzan.e: Sho Hashi of Chuzan attacked Nakijin in 1416 with the help of disaffected Hokuzan lords; King Hananchi killed himself. Chuzan then appointed a warden to govern the north.

hellenic-alliance.t: The alliance of Greek states, led by Sparta, that defeated the invasion of Xerxes at Salamis, Plataea and Mycale in 480-479 BCE.
hellenic-alliance.o: In autumn 481 BCE, as the Persian king Xerxes gathered his army in Asia Minor, delegates of the Greek states willing to resist met at the Isthmus of Corinth. They swore an alliance, ended their own feuds, including the war between Athens and Aegina, and sent envoys to seek help from Argos, Syracuse, Corcyra and Crete, with little success.
hellenic-alliance.r: The alliance had a council of delegates (probouloi) meeting at the Isthmus, but command lay with Sparta, which led on land and, through Eurybiades, at sea, although Themistocles' Athenian fleet was the largest. Some 31 states are named on the Serpent Column dedicated at Delphi after the war. Members who had sided with Persia were threatened with punishment.
hellenic-alliance.e: After victories at Salamis (480 BCE) and Plataea and Mycale (479 BCE), the Greeks carried the war to the Aegean. The arrogance of the Spartan regent Pausanias at Byzantium in 478 BCE led the Ionian allies to turn to Athens, which founded the Delian League. The alliance itself lingered formally until 461 BCE.

hutsul-republic.t: A short-lived republic of Hutsul highlanders in the Carpathians, which declared for union with Ukraine after the fall of Austria-Hungary.
hutsul-republic.o: In November 1918, as Hungarian rule over Transcarpathia collapsed, a council of Hutsuls in the mountain village of Yasinia took power locally. In January 1919 it proclaimed its wish to join the Ukrainian People's Republic, with Stepan Klochurak leading the local government.
hutsul-republic.r: The republic was a small highland territory of shepherds, woodcutters and rafters, run by an elected council and defended by a few hundred armed volunteers. It drove off Hungarian troops and tried to keep in contact with the West Ukrainian People's Republic across the mountains, but it had little means of survival on its own.
hutsul-republic.e: In June 1919 Romanian troops occupied Yasinia and ended the republic. The Treaty of Saint-Germain then assigned Transcarpathia to Czechoslovakia, and the region later formed Carpatho-Ukraine. The Hutsul Republic is remembered as an early expression of Ukrainian national feeling in Transcarpathia.

herakleopolitan-kingdom.t: The Ninth and Tenth Dynasties of Herakleopolis, which ruled northern Egypt in the First Intermediate Period and fought Thebes for the throne.
herakleopolitan-kingdom.o: Around 2160 BCE a family from Herakleopolis Magna, near the entrance to the Faiyum, took over the kingship from the Eighth Dynasty of Egypt. Its founder, remembered as Meryibre Khety (Akhtoy), gave his name to the 'House of Khety', which held Middle Egypt and the Delta.
herakleopolitan-kingdom.r: The Herakleopolitan kings depended on powerful provincial governors, notably the nomarchs of Asyut, whose tomb inscriptions record the war against the south. The literary text known as the Teaching for Merikare, set in this period, gives advice on kingship, justice and defending the Delta frontier against Asiatics. Middle Egyptian literature, later regarded as classical, began to take shape in this age.
herakleopolitan-kingdom.e: From about 2130 BCE the kings fought the Theban Eleventh Dynasty for control of Thinis and Abydos. Around 2025 BCE Mentuhotep II of Thebes took Herakleopolis and reunited Egypt, opening the Middle Kingdom of Egypt.

habr-yunis-sultanate.t: A Somali sultanate of the Habr Yunis clan that broke away from the Isaaq Sultanate and played a part in the early Dervish movement.
habr-yunis-sultanate.o: The Habr Yunis, one of the Isaaq clans, set up their own sultanate around 1787, breaking away from the Isaaq Sultanate after a dispute over succession and authority. Its sultans were based near Toon and later in the area of Burao in northern Somalia.
habr-yunis-sultanate.r: Like other Somali sultanates it was a clan polity, with the sultan presiding over elders and mediating conflicts according to customary and Islamic law. Its people herded camels and traded through Berbera. Sultan Nur Ahmed Aman was among the leaders who opposed British and missionary influence and joined Mohammed Abdullah Hassan in founding the Dervish movement in the 1890s.
habr-yunis-sultanate.e: The Habr Yunis signed protection treaties with Britain in the 1880s and became part of British Somaliland. The sultanate's political role faded in the early 20th century, though the title survives as a traditional office.

hindu-shahis.t: The last Hindu dynasty of Kabul and Gandhara, which held the north-western gateway of India until Mahmud of Ghazni's invasions.
hindu-shahis.o: Around 822 Kallar, a Brahmin minister of the last Turk Shahis, overthrew his master and founded a new dynasty. The Hindu Shahis ruled from Kabul and, after its loss to the Saffarids around 870, from Udabhandapura (Hund) on the Indus.
hindu-shahis.r: The Shahis ruled a Hindu and Buddhist population from the Kabul valley to the Punjab. Their silver 'bull and horseman' coins, showing Shiva's bull Nandi and a mounted warrior, were imitated widely across northern India and Central Asia. They maintained alliances with Kashmir and built temples in the Salt Range, and al-Biruni later praised their noble conduct.
hindu-shahis.e: The Ghaznavid Empire launched repeated invasions: Jayapala was defeated by Sabuktigin and then by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1001 at Peshawar, after which he committed suicide. His successors Anandapala and Trilochanapala lost further battles, and the dynasty ended by 1026 with the last Shahi kings in exile in Kashmir.

hammadid-emirate.t: A Berber dynasty of central Algeria whose fortified capital, the Qal'at Beni Hammad, is now a World Heritage site.
hammadid-emirate.o: Hammad ibn Buluggin, a son of the Zirid founder, governed the western lands of the Zirid emirate and founded the fortified city of Qal'at Beni Hammad in the Hodna mountains around 1007 to 1008. In 1015 he broke with his nephew, the Zirid emir Badis, and founded an independent dynasty.
hammadid-emirate.r: The Hammadid capital grew into a city of palaces, mosques and workshops, with a great minaret and fine glazed ceramics. The emirs ruled the central Maghreb, drawing on Sanhaja Berber tribes. Pressure from the Banu Hilal led al-Nasir ibn Alnas to build a new capital at Béjaïa (Bougie) on the coast in the 1060s, which became a busy port trading with Italian cities.
hammadid-emirate.e: In 1152 the Almohad Caliphate under Abd al-Mu'min took Béjaïa and the Qal'a, and the last emir, Yahya ibn al-Aziz, surrendered. Béjaïa remained a centre of learning and trade, and the ruins of the Qal'a were listed as a World Heritage site in 1980.

hispania-ulterior.t: Rome's province of Further Spain, covering the rich south and west of Iberia from 197 BCE until Augustus split it into Baetica and Lusitania.
hispania-ulterior.o: After driving Carthage out of Iberia in 206 BCE, Rome first governed the conquered south through commanders. In 197 BCE it created two provinces, each under a praetor; Hispania Ulterior covered the Guadalquivir valley and the lands to the west, including Gades and the former territory of the Turdetani.
hispania-ulterior.r: Governors based at Corduba, founded by Marcus Claudius Marcellus in the 2nd century BCE, commanded armies and collected tribute from Iberian and Phoenician towns. Silver mining, oil and grain made it rich, while campaigns against the Lusitanians dominated the 2nd century BCE. Julius Caesar served there as quaestor and then governor in 61 BCE.
hispania-ulterior.e: In the civil wars it was a stronghold of the Pompeians, defeated by Caesar at Munda in 45 BCE. From 27 BCE Augustus reorganised it into Hispania Baetica and Lusitania, though the formal division took several years.

hiroshima-domain.t: A large domain on the Inland Sea, ruled by the Asano family from Hiroshima castle for two and a half centuries.
hiroshima-domain.o: When the Mori were reduced to Choshu after Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu gave Aki and Bingo to Fukushima Masanori in 1600. In 1619 the shogunate dismissed Masanori for repairing the flood-damaged castle without permission, and transferred Asano Nagaakira to Hiroshima with about 426,000 koku.
hiroshima-domain.r: The Asano ruled the domain until its abolition. Hiroshima, built on the delta of the Ota river, grew into a major castle town and port. The domain profited from rice, salt pans, oyster farming in Hiroshima Bay and paper, and controlled the shrine island of Itsukushima. The Shukkeien garden was laid out for Nagaakira from 1620.
hiroshima-domain.e: Hiroshima served as a base for the shogunate's expeditions against neighbouring Choshu in the 1860s but sought mediation and joined the imperial side in 1868. After abolition in 1871 it became Hiroshima Prefecture.

hispania-tarraconensis.t: The largest Roman province in Hispania, stretching from the Pyrenees to Galicia, governed from Tarraco for nearly five centuries.
hispania-tarraconensis.o: Tarraconensis was formed by Augustus from 27 BCE out of Hispania Citerior, enlarged with the north-west after the Cantabrian Wars. Augustus wintered at Tarraco in 26 to 25 BCE, and the city became the seat of the governor and of the imperial cult for the province.
hispania-tarraconensis.r: It was an imperial province under a senatorial legate, with the Legio VII Gemina based at León to guard the gold mines of the north-west. Tarraco had a great provincial forum and circus. The province contained hundreds of towns, from Caesaraugusta to Barcino, and exported wine, oil and minerals. Its legate Galba was proclaimed emperor here in 68 CE. Under Diocletian around 293 it was split into Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis and Gallaecia.
hispania-tarraconensis.e: The reduced province remained Roman longest in Hispania, despite Bagaudae revolts in the 5th century. Tarraco fell to the Visigothic king Euric in the early 470s, ending Roman rule in Iberia.

histria.t: The oldest Greek colony on the western Black Sea coast, founded by Miletus near the mouth of the Danube.
histria.o: Milesian colonists founded Histria c. 657 BCE on a peninsula by the sea near the Danube delta, in modern Dobruja, Romania. It was named after the Istros, the Greek name for the Danube, and became the earliest Greek city on the western Black Sea coast.
histria.r: Histria traded olive oil, wine and pottery with the Getae and Scythians for grain, fish, honey and slaves. Aristotle mentions its shift from oligarchy to democracy. Its sanctuaries honoured Zeus Polieus and Aphrodite, and it struck silver coins showing two heads and a sea eagle catching a dolphin.
histria.e: Histria was garrisoned by Lysimachus and revolted against him in 313 BCE. Its harbour silted up. In 72 to 71 BCE Marcus Lucullus brought the western Pontic cities under Roman control, and Burebista's Getae sacked the city soon after. It revived under Rome and was abandoned in the 7th century CE.

hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.t: The Caribbean islands owned by the Knights of Malta, a crusading order that briefly ran Saint Kitts, Saint Martin, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint Croix.
hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.o: Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy, a Knight of Malta and governor-general of the French Antilles, persuaded the order to buy the French shares of Saint Kitts, Saint Martin, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint Croix from the bankrupt Compagnie des Îles d'Amérique. The purchase, approved by Grand Master Jean-Paul Lascaris-Castellar and Louis XIV, was completed in 1651.
hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.r: Poincy governed the islands from his château near Basseterre on Saint Kitts as the order's lieutenant, while the French crown kept sovereignty. It was the only overseas colony the Hospitallers ever held. The economy rested on tobacco and early sugar, with enslaved Africans as labour. Saint-Barthélemy's settlement was destroyed by the Kalinago in 1656. After Poincy's death in 1660, Charles de Sales succeeded him.
hospitaller-caribbean-colonies.e: The venture never paid the distant order much. In 1665 the knights sold their rights to the new French West India Company of Jean-Baptiste Colbert, returning the islands to ordinary French colonial rule. The episode left little trace beyond Poincy's buildings.

hierapytna.t: South Cretan port city that grew into the dominant power of eastern Crete in the Hellenistic age, destroying Praisos and contesting lands with Itanos.
hierapytna.o: Hierapytna lay at the narrowest point of eastern Crete, on the south coast at modern Ierapetra. Founded in the early Iron Age, it was a modest town in the Classical period and grew strong only in the Hellenistic age.
hierapytna.r: Hierapytna made treaties with Rhodes and with Hellenistic kings, supplying mercenaries and ships. It expanded aggressively, destroying Praisos c. 145 BCE and claiming the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus against Itanos. Rome arbitrated the dispute in the late 2nd century BCE. The city was also accused of harbouring pirates.
hierapytna.e: Hierapytna was among the last Cretan cities to fall to Metellus in 67 BCE. Rebuilt as a Roman port, it prospered with theatres and baths, and survives as the town of Ierapetra.

hirosaki-domain.t: The domain of the Tsugaru family at the northern tip of Honshu, founded by a vassal who broke away from the Nanbu.
hirosaki-domain.o: Oura Tamenobu, a vassal of the Nanbu, seized the Tsugaru region in the 1570s and 1580s and won recognition directly from Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1590, taking the name Tsugaru. His son Nobuhira completed Hirosaki castle in 1611.
hirosaki-domain.r: The breakaway left lasting enmity with the Nanbu of Morioka. The domain opened new rice land, but its cold climate made harvests unreliable, and the Tenmei famine of the 1780s killed a large share of the population. The fourth lord, Tsugaru Nobumasa, carried out reforms, and the domain later provided guards for Ezo against Russian incursions.
hirosaki-domain.e: In the Boshin War Hirosaki first joined the Ouetsu Reppan Domei but switched to the imperial side in 1868. After the abolition of domains in 1871 it became part of Aomori Prefecture; Hirosaki castle's keep survives.

himyarite-kingdom.t: The last great kingdom of ancient Yemen, which unified south Arabia, adopted Judaism as a state faith and fell to Aksum in 525.
himyarite-kingdom.o: Himyar emerged in the highlands south of the Kingdom of Saba; its era, used for dating, began around 110 BCE. From the capital Zafar its kings, styled kings of Saba and Dhu Raydan, fought Saba for centuries. Shammar Yahrish absorbed Saba around 275 CE and the Kingdom of Hadramawt around 300, uniting all of south Arabia.
himyarite-kingdom.r: Himyar controlled ports and the incense lands and, under Abikarib As'ad in the 5th century, extended its authority into central Arabia through the Kingdom of Kinda. Around 380 its rulers abandoned the old gods for a monotheism close to Judaism, and inscriptions to the Merciful replaced those to Almaqah. Marib Dam repairs and highland terracing sustained a dense agricultural population.
himyarite-kingdom.e: King Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar, known in Arab tradition as Dhu Nuwas, persecuted the Christians of Najran in 523. In 525 the Aksumite Empire invaded under Kaleb, Yusuf was killed and Aksumite Yemen took its place. Himyarite memory shaped later Yemeni identity and genealogy.

hapalla.t: Hapalla, one of the small Luwian vassal kingdoms created by the Hittites from the defeated land of Arzawa.
hapalla.o: Hapalla lay in western or south-western Anatolia, on the eastern side of the Arzawa lands, perhaps in later Pisidia. After Mursili II of the Hittite Empire defeated Arzawa c. 1320 BCE, he made Targasnalli king of Hapalla.
hapalla.r: Known almost only from the treaty between Mursili II and Targasnalli, which bound the king to send troops, return fugitives and remain loyal. Its people spoke Luwian.
hapalla.e: Hapalla stayed a Hittite vassal until the empire collapsed c. 1180 BCE, after which it disappears from the record.

hecatomnid-caria.t: Hecatomnid Caria, a Persian satrapy ruled as a dynastic kingdom by Mausolus and his family, whose tomb gave the world the word mausoleum.
hecatomnid-caria.o: Hecatomnus of Mylasa, a Carian noble, was made satrap of Caria by the Achaemenid Empire c. 395 BCE. He founded a dynasty that governed south-western Anatolia almost as independent kings while acknowledging Persian authority.
hecatomnid-caria.r: His son Mausolus moved the capital to Halicarnassus, extended control over Lycia and the islands, and combined Carian and Greek culture. After his death his sister-wife Artemisia II completed his tomb, the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders. Siblings married each other and inherited power in turn, including Idrieus and Ada.
hecatomnid-caria.e: Pixodarus pushed his sister Ada aside, but in 334 BCE Alexander of the Macedonian Empire besieged Halicarnassus and restored Ada, who adopted him as her son. Caria then passed to the Hellenistic kingdoms.

heraclea-lucania.t: Greek city founded jointly by Taras and Thurii in 433 BCE, seat of the Italiote League and site of Pyrrhus's first victory over Rome.
heraclea-lucania.o: After Taras and Thurii fought over the territory of ruined Siris, they settled the dispute by founding a new city together in 433 or 432 BCE, with Taras taking the lead. Heraclea was built on a plateau near the Siris and Aciris rivers, at modern Policoro.
heraclea-lucania.r: Heraclea was dominated by Taras, which moved the meeting place of the Italiote League there in the 4th century BCE, and it held the league's festival. The city prospered from farming the coastal plain. The bronze Tables of Heraclea, found in 1732, record on one side Greek temple land surveys and on the other a Roman municipal law of the 1st century BCE.
heraclea-lucania.e: In 280 BCE Pyrrhus defeated the Romans under Laevinus at Heraclea, using elephants. In 278 BCE Heraclea made a treaty with Rome on very favourable terms. It became a Roman municipium after the Social War and declined in late antiquity.

huanca.t: A confederation of highland peoples in Peru's Mantaro valley who fought among themselves until conquered by the Incas, and later allied with the Spanish.
huanca.o: After the Wari Empire collapsed, the Mantaro valley in central Peru was divided among the Huanca, or Wanka, and related groups such as the Xauxa. From about 1000 they formed communities of chiefdoms, and in the 14th century fortified hilltop towns such as Tunanmarca and Hatunmarca grew to house thousands.
huanca.r: The Huanca were divided into rival groups led by local war leaders called sinchis, and their hilltop towns reflect frequent warfare. They farmed potatoes and other tubers, grew maize in lower valleys and herded llamas. The valley was one of the most productive in the central Andes, and Hatun Xauxa later became a major Inca centre.
huanca.e: The Incas conquered the Huanca around 1460, resettling them in valley-floor villages. In 1533 Huanca lords allied with Francisco Pizarro and supplied his troops; they later petitioned the Spanish crown for rewards. Jauja was briefly the Spanish capital in 1534.
huanca.re: Huanca religion, cult of Wari Willka

hotak-dynasty.t: A Ghilji Pashtun dynasty from Kandahar that threw off Safavid rule and, under Mahmud Hotak, captured Isfahan and toppled the Safavid dynasty in 1722.
hotak-dynasty.o: In 1709 Mirwais Hotak, a chief of the Ghilji Pashtuns, led a revolt in Kandahar against the Safavid governor Gurgin Khan, killed him and made Kandahar independent. He repelled Safavid attempts to retake the city and ruled until his death in 1715.
hotak-dynasty.r: Mirwais governed with the support of Pashtun tribal councils and avoided the title of king. His son Mahmud Hotak invaded Persia, defeated the Safavid army at Gulnabad in 1722 and took Isfahan after a long siege, forcing Shah Sultan Husayn to abdicate. Hotak rule in Persia was harsh and insecure, and Mahmud's successor Ashraf faced Ottoman and Russian advances as well as Safavid loyalists.
hotak-dynasty.e: Nader Shah, fighting for the Safavid pretender Tahmasp II, defeated Ashraf at Damghan in 1729 and drove the Afghans out of Persia. In 1738 Nader besieged and took Kandahar from Hussain Hotak, ending the dynasty. Its fall cleared the way for the later Durrani Empire.

hernici.t: Italic people of the Sacco valley in southern Latium, long-time allies of Rome whose towns are known for their massive polygonal walls.
hernici.o: The Hernici lived in the hills of the middle Sacco valley, between the Latins, the Volsci and the Aequi. Their name was explained from a Marsic word for rocks. They were an Italic people, probably related to the Sabellians, organised by the 5th century BCE in a league of towns centred on Anagnia.
hernici.r: Their towns, Anagnia, Ferentinum, Aletrium and Verulae, met in league councils at the Maritime Circus near Anagnia. Aletrium's acropolis with its huge polygonal walls is among the best preserved in Italy. Wedged between the Volsci and Aequi, the Hernici made a treaty with Rome and the Latins, traditionally in 486 BCE, and fought alongside them for much of the 5th century.
hernici.e: Relations broke down in the 4th century. In 306 BCE Anagnia led a revolt and was punished with citizenship without the vote, while Ferentinum, Aletrium and Verulae, which stayed loyal, kept their independence as allies. All became Roman municipia after the Social War.

hocaba.t: A small Maya province of north-central Yucatán, one of the territories that emerged after the fall of Mayapan in the 1440s.
hocaba.o: Hocabá was one of the provinces (kuchkabalob) formed in northern Yucatán after the League of Mayapan collapsed around 1441. It occupied a compact area south-east of present-day Mérida, between Ceh Pech, Ah Kin Chel and Sotuta.
hocaba.r: The province was governed from the town of Hocabá by a ruler of the Iuit lineage, who held authority over the batabs, the heads of individual towns such as Homún. Like its neighbours, it lived from maize farming, beekeeping and cotton weaving. It is known mainly from Spanish colonial records studied by Ralph Roys.
hocaba.e: Hocabá submitted to the Spanish in the early 1540s and was absorbed into the Province of Yucatán. Its towns became colonial encomiendas.

herero-paramountcy.t: The cattle-rich Herero chieftaincy of Okahandja, whose 1904 rising against German rule ended in genocide.
herero-paramountcy.o: The Herero, Bantu-speaking cattle herders of central Namibia, had been raided for decades by Jonker Afrikaner's Orlam Afrikaner State. In 1863 they rose under Kamaherero, known as Maharero, at Otjimbingwe and won their independence, confirmed by the Peace of Okahandja in 1870.
herero-paramountcy.r: Maharero made Okahandja the seat of a paramountcy over many Herero chiefs, though authority was shared with lineage heads. Wealth lay in vast herds, and the holy fire of each homestead linked the living with ancestors. Rhenish missionaries were active, and in 1885 Maharero signed a protection treaty with Germany; Samuel Maharero succeeded him in 1890.
herero-paramountcy.e: Land loss, debt and abuses under German South West Africa led to the Herero rising in January 1904. After the battle of Waterberg, General von Trotha ordered their extermination; most Herero died in the Omaheke desert or in camps.

hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.t: The kingdom of the Hashemite dynasty east of the Jordan, which has survived regional wars and hosts millions of refugees.
hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.o: Britain ended its mandate over the Emirate of Transjordan on 25 May 1946, and the emir Abdullah I became king. In the 1948 war the Arab Legion held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, which Jordan annexed in 1950.
hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.r: Jordan is a constitutional monarchy in which the king holds wide powers. Abdullah I was assassinated in Jerusalem in 1951; after the brief reign of Talal, Hussein ruled from 1953 to 1999. Jordan lost the West Bank to Israel in 1967 and expelled the Palestinian armed groups in the conflict of Black September in 1970. It has relied on foreign aid, phosphates and remittances, and its population is largely of Palestinian origin.
hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan.e: Hussein signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994. His son Abdullah II succeeded him in 1999 and has kept the monarchy stable while hosting large numbers of Iraqi and Syrian refugees.

helian-xia.t: The Xiongnu kingdom of Helian Bobo, builder of the white-walled city of Tongwan on the edge of the Ordos desert, which briefly took Chang'an from the Jin.
helian-xia.o: Liu Bobo, of the Tiefu Xiongnu, was a commander under Later Qin who broke away in 407 and proclaimed himself Heavenly King of Great Xia, claiming descent from the ancient Xia dynasty. He later took the surname Helian.
helian-xia.r: Helian Bobo's mobile cavalry raided Later Qin ruthlessly. Between 413 and 418 he built the capital Tongwan, its walls of pounded earth mixed with lime so hard that, it was said, builders were executed if an awl could pierce them; its white ruins survive in northern Shaanxi. In 418 he captured Chang'an from the Eastern Jin forces left by Liu Yu.
helian-xia.e: After Helian Bobo's death in 425, Northern Wei took Tongwan in 427 and captured Helian Chang. His brother Helian Ding destroyed Western Qin in 431 but was captured by the Tuyuhun while crossing the Yellow River and handed to the Wei.

hsipaw-state.t: A northern Shan state on the Dokhtawady river whose last ruler, Sao Kya Seng, disappeared after the Burmese military coup of 1962.
hsipaw-state.o: Hsipaw, Shan Thibaw, was founded as a Shan principality in the Dokhtawady valley of the northern Shan plateau; tradition dates its ruling house to the 14th century. For long periods it was associated with the larger state of Onbaung, whose name it sometimes used.
hsipaw-state.r: The saopha of Hsipaw ruled from a haw, or palace, overseeing rice and tea growing and trade along the road from Mandalay to China. Hsipaw was a tributary of the Burmese crown and supplied consorts to the royal court. Sao Hkun Hseng, ruler from 1886, cooperated with the British and modernised his state.
hsipaw-state.e: Hsipaw became one of the British protected Shan states and joined the Federated Shan States in 1922. Its ruler surrendered powers in 1959. The last saopha, Sao Kya Seng, and his Austrian wife Inge Sargent, whose memoir told their story, were victims of the 1962 coup; he disappeared in army custody.

huron-confederacy.t: An alliance of Wendat nations between Lake Simcoe and Georgian Bay, the hub of the early French fur trade until Iroquois attacks dispersed it in 1649.
huron-confederacy.o: Wendat tradition holds that the Bear and Cord nations formed a league around 1440, joined by the Rock nation around 1590 and the Deer around 1610. Their country, Wendake or Huronia, lay in what is now Simcoe County, Ontario, where 20,000 to 30,000 people lived in palisaded villages of longhouses, among them Ossossane, the main town of the Bear.
huron-confederacy.r: A confederacy council of village and clan chiefs met to settle disputes and decide on war and trade, and the Feast of the Dead united communities through shared reburial of their dead. Women controlled fields of maize, beans and squash, whose surplus the Wendat traded north to Algonquian hunters for furs. Allied with New France from Champlain's visit in 1615, they hosted Jesuit missions, including Sainte-Marie among the Hurons, founded in 1639.
huron-confederacy.e: Epidemics in the 1630s halved the population, and in 1648 to 1649 the Iroquois Confederacy destroyed the main towns and killed missionaries such as Jean de Brébeuf. Survivors fled; some settled near Quebec, where Wendake survives, and others joined the Petun to become the Wyandot.

hasanwayhid-dynasty.t: A Kurdish dynasty that ruled the western Zagros under Buyid overlordship and was praised for the security of its roads and its charity.
hasanwayhid-dynasty.o: Hasanwayh ibn Husayn, a chief of the Kurdish Barzikani tribe, took control of the mountains around Dinavar, Hamadan, Nahavand and Shahrizor in 959, as Buyid power was still being consolidated. His stronghold was the fortress of Sarmaj near Bisotun.
hasanwayhid-dynasty.r: Hasanwayh paid tribute to the Buyid dynasty while ruling his tribal domains independently. His son Badr ibn Hasanwayh (979 to 1014), given the title Nasir al-Dawla by the caliph, became the most famous of the line. He was praised by chroniclers for building mosques and caravanserais, protecting the pilgrim road and subsidising the poor and the holy cities, while keeping order among the Kurdish tribes.
hasanwayhid-dynasty.e: Badr was killed by his own troops in 1014. Shams al-Dawla, the Buyid ruler of Hamadan, and the Kakuyid dynasty soon took over his territories, and the Hasanwayhids disappeared by 1015, partly replaced by the Annazid dynasty.

heungyo.t: A brief attempt to revive Balhae, proclaimed at Liaoyang in 1029 by a descendant of its founder in revolt against the Khitan Liao dynasty.
heungyo.o: In 1029 Dae Yeon-rim, a descendant of Balhae's founder Dae Joyeong serving as an officer of the Liao dynasty at Dongjing, modern Liaoyang, rebelled against Khitan rule, killed local officials and proclaimed a new state called Heungyo, Xingliao in Chinese, with its own era name.
heungyo.r: The rebellion drew on Balhae descendants in the Liaodong region who resented Khitan taxes and labour demands. Dae Yeon-rim sent envoys to Goryeo asking for help, but Goryeo declined to intervene.
heungyo.e: Liao armies besieged Dongjing, and in 1030 an officer opened the city gates; Dae Yeon-rim was captured and the state ended after about a year. Some of his followers fled to Goryeo.

huastec-chiefdoms.t: The independent lordships of the Huastec (Teenek) people on the north-east Gulf Coast of Mexico, speakers of a Maya language long separated from the rest.
huastec-chiefdoms.o: The Huastec separated from other Maya speakers well over two thousand years ago and settled the lowlands of northern Veracruz, San Luis Potosí and Tamaulipas. From around 900 their region was organised into numerous small lordships centred on towns with circular platforms.
huastec-chiefdoms.r: Each lordship was led by its own chief, and there was no unified state. The Huastec were known for shell ornaments, distinctive black-on-white pottery and sculptures of youthful deities such as the Huastec Adolescent. The fertile Huasteca produced cotton and textiles. Mexica sources viewed them as foreign and depicted them with prejudice.
huastec-chiefdoms.e: From the 1450s the Aztec Empire conquered much of the Huasteca and demanded tribute. Hernán Cortés subdued the region in 1522, and slave raiding under Nuño de Guzmán devastated it. The Teenek people survive and their language is still spoken.

hedmark.t: Inland kingdom around Lake Mjøsa, one of the core lands of Halfdan the Black, where petty kings survived until Olaf Haraldsson.
hedmark.o: Hedmark, the farming land on the eastern shore of Lake Mjøsa, was one of the richest districts of inland Norway. The sagas say Halfdan the Black of Vestfold gained it by war and inheritance in the 9th century, making it part of the base from which Harald Fairhair built his kingdom.
hedmark.r: Hedmark's wealth came from grain, cattle and iron from the surrounding forests. It shared the Eidsivating law assembly with the other Uppland districts. Local kings kept their position under the high kings, and the sagas name Hrørek as king of Hedmark in the early 11th century.
hedmark.e: Around 1018 Olaf Haraldsson crushed a revolt of the Uppland kings and had Hrørek blinded, ending the line of local kings. Hedmark became part of the Kingdom of Norway, and Hamar, on Lake Mjøsa, became the seat of a bishop in 1152.

harfush-emirate.t: A Shia dynasty of emirs who governed Baalbek and the northern Beqaa Valley under the Ottomans for more than three centuries.
harfush-emirate.o: The Harfush were a Twelver Shia clan who held Baalbek and its district by the early Ottoman period. The Ottomans, who conquered Syria in 1516, confirmed them as local governors and tax farmers, a role the family kept for generations.
harfush-emirate.r: The emirs collected taxes from the farmers of the Beqaa and passed revenue to the governors of Damascus, keeping their own armed retainers. Their politics turned on rivalry and alliance with the Druze Ma'nids and later the Shihabis of the Mount Lebanon Emirate. Yunus al-Harfush allied with Fakhr al-Din II before falling out with him; he was executed in 1625. The family protected the Shia community of the Beqaa.
harfush-emirate.e: Internal feuds and conflict with the Shihabis weakened them in the 19th century. During the Tanzimat reforms the Ottomans removed the last emirs and exiled the family in the 1860s.

halogaland.t: The far northern chieftaincy of Viking Age Norway, home of the traveller Ohthere and of powerful lords who traded furs with the Sámi.
halogaland.o: Hålogaland stretched along the Norwegian coast north of Trøndelag, including the Lofoten islands. Its chieftains grew rich in the Iron Age: the great longhouse at Borg in Lofoten, over 80 metres long, was the seat of a local lord from the 6th century.
halogaland.r: The Hålogaland lords controlled trade in furs, walrus ivory, hides and dried fish, much of it taken as tribute from the Sámi. Around 890 Ohthere, a Hålogaland chieftain, described his life and his voyage round the North Cape to King Alfred of Wessex, the earliest written account of the region. Power rested on chieftains rather than a formal kingdom.
halogaland.e: In the late 9th century the region came under Harald Fairhair and the earls of Lade, whose family is said to have come from Hålogaland. Local magnates such as Tore Hund remained powerful into the 11th century, before the area was fully integrated into the Kingdom of Norway.

hungarian-tribal-federation.t: Confederation of seven Magyar tribes in the steppe of Etelköz, under Khazar overlordship, that set off to conquer the Carpathian basin in 895.
hungarian-tribal-federation.o: The Hungarians, Finno-Ugric speakers who had absorbed steppe Turkic culture, moved west and by about 830 lived in Etelköz, between the Dnieper and the lower Danube. Constantine VII describes seven tribes led first by Levedi, under the authority of the Khazar Khaganate.
hungarian-tribal-federation.r: They were mounted pastoralists and fearsome raiders, selling captives to traders on the Black Sea. Leadership was dual, with a sacral kende and a military gyula. Three Kabar tribes, rebels from the Khazars, joined them. They raided East Francia from 862 and fought for Byzantium against Bulgaria in 894. Álmos and then his son Árpád were elected as leaders.
hungarian-tribal-federation.e: In 895 Pechenegs and Bulgarians attacked Etelköz, and the Hungarians crossed the Carpathians into the basin, founding the Principality of Hungary.

habbari-dynasty.t: An Arab dynasty that ruled lower Sindh from al-Mansura as nominal vassals of the Abbasids until Mahmud of Ghazni ended it.
habbari-dynasty.o: Sindh had been an Umayyad and then Abbasid province since the conquest by Muhammad ibn Qasim in 711 to 712. As Abbasid control weakened, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Habbari, from an Arab family settled in Sindh, made himself ruler around 854 at al-Mansura, the provincial capital near modern Shahdadpur, while continuing to recognise the caliph.
habbari-dynasty.r: The Habbari emirs ruled lower Sindh while the Emirate of Multan held the north. Arab geographers such as al-Masudi and Ibn Hawqal visited al-Mansura and described a prosperous city with a large mosque, where Arabic and Sindhi were spoken and trade passed between the Indus and the Persian Gulf. The ruling elite was Sunni Muslim, while much of the population remained Hindu and Buddhist.
habbari-dynasty.e: Around 1026 Mahmud of Ghazni attacked al-Mansura, reportedly because its ruler had adopted Ismaili beliefs, and deposed the Habbari emir. Sindh came under the Ghaznavids, and soon after the Soomra dynasty rose to power.
